name: Capture
definition: Observe and capture organizational reality
purpose: Collect organizational signals; preserve source information
inputs: People; Meetings; Emails; Chats; Systems; Documents; Workflows; Events
outputs: Raw activity; Raw events; Raw communications; Raw organizational signals
plain_english: The Capture layer is the Brain's sensory system — it observes and records everything your organization does: every email, Slack message, meeting, document, workflow, and event. It does not interpret or judge what anything means yet. Its only job is to ensure nothing gets missed. Think of it as the ears and eyes of the organization — capturing raw signals before any analysis begins.
example: A team meeting happens on Zoom. An email thread about a client is exchanged. A Slack message assigns a task to someone. A contract document is uploaded to a shared drive. A workflow runs in your CRM. All of these are captured as raw signals — audio, text, documents, system events — before any interpretation occurs. None of it is understood yet; it's simply preserved as the raw material for the Understanding layer.

name: Understanding
definition: Transform activity into organizational understanding
purpose: Identify atomic primitives in every signal; produce Canonical Knowledge Objects
outputs: Structured organizational reality as Canonical Knowledge Objects
plain_english: The Understanding layer reads all the raw captured activity and asks: what does this actually mean in terms of how the organization works? It identifies the atomic building blocks present in every signal — who was involved (Actors), what was communicated (Communication), what was promised (Commitment), what was done (Action), what was used (Resource), what rule applied (Rule), what was being achieved (Goal) — and packages them into structured Knowledge Objects that the rest of the Brain can work with. This is where raw activity becomes structured organizational reality.
example: From the Zoom meeting captured earlier, Understanding reads the transcript and identifies: Sarah (Actor) made a commitment (Commitment primitive) to deliver the client proposal (Resource) to Acme Corp (Actor) by Friday (Time). It packages this as a Commitment Object — structured, typed, and traceable to the meeting where it was made. The meeting discussion itself becomes a Communication Object. The client relationship becomes a Relationship. All of this is now machine-readable and ready to be remembered.

name: Memory
definition: Preserve organizational understanding through time
purpose: Maintain five memory stores; attach provenance; serve memory to Intelligence
plain_english: The Memory layer takes the Knowledge Objects produced by Understanding and routes them into five specialized memory stores, each optimized for a different kind of organizational knowledge. This is the Brain's actual long-term memory — the organizational knowledge that persists through time, survives staff turnover, and can be retrieved weeks or years later to answer questions, reconstruct decisions, or check the status of commitments. Memory is not a database of documents — it is a structured, provenance-tagged, living record of organizational reality.
example: The Commitment Object from Sarah's promise goes into Commitment Memory with status 'Promised', owner 'Sarah', due date 'Friday'. The meeting discussion goes into Interaction Memory — capturing who was present, what was discussed, and what reasoning led to the commitment. Sarah's profile as an Account Executive goes into Factual Memory. The Acme client goes into Factual Memory as an Actor. All records are linked together and carry provenance: source, timestamp, author. The Brain can now answer 'what did Sarah promise in that meeting?' with certainty.

name: Intelligence
definition: Transform memory into organizational intelligence
purpose: Reason over memory; detect patterns; identify risks; generate recommendations
plain_english: The Intelligence layer reads all five memory stores and reasons over them to generate insights humans and AI can act on. It does not just retrieve information — it thinks about it. It detects patterns, identifies risks before they become problems, spots opportunities before the window closes, flags when reality is drifting from what was planned, generates concrete recommendations, and scores organizational health. Intelligence is the layer that transforms the Brain from a record-keeper into a reasoning partner.
example: Intelligence reads Commitment Memory and notices that Sarah's proposal commitment is now 2 days past the Friday deadline with no status update recorded in Action Memory. It cross-references Goal Memory and finds the Acme account is linked to a $200k Q3 revenue target. Operational Risk generated: 'Commitment COMM-089 at risk of breach — no progress recorded, deadline passed. Owner: Sarah's Manager Maria. Confidence: High. Related Goal: Q3 Revenue Target.' Maria receives this risk alert before her Monday morning starts.

name: Execution
definition: Transform intelligence into action
purpose: Execute work; coordinate activity; complete commitments
plain_english: The Execution layer is where intelligence becomes action — where humans and AI agents do the actual work. This includes responding to recommendations, completing tasks, running automated workflows, coordinating across teams, and making decisions. Every action taken at this layer gets recorded back into Memory, creating a continuous loop: execution generates new organizational reality, which becomes new memory, which generates new intelligence. The Brain does not execute instead of humans and agents — it executes alongside them, informed by everything it knows.
example: Sarah's manager Maria receives the Operational Risk alert about the overdue Acme proposal. She schedules a check-in call with Sarah (human action — Action Memory records it). A Brain agent automatically retrieves the full Acme commitment history and drafts a follow-up email to the client acknowledging the delay and providing an updated timeline (agent action — also recorded in Action Memory). Both actions update the commitment status and feed new learning signals back into the Evolution layer.

name: Exposure
definition: Deliver memory and intelligence to humans and AI through appropriate channels
purpose: Ambient delivery; agent access; mission control delivery; context injection
outputs: Slack suggestions; Email context; Calendar briefs; MCP responses; Reality feed items
plain_english: The Exposure layer is how the Brain delivers memory and intelligence to the right person at the right moment through the right channel — without requiring anyone to go searching. The Brain does not wait to be asked; it surfaces relevant context wherever work is already happening: inside Gmail as you compose an email, inside Slack as a message thread develops, in your calendar before a meeting begins, inside Claude or ChatGPT as an AI agent builds a response. The v2 product philosophy is that the Brain is infrastructure — it comes to you, not the other way around.
example: When Maria opens Gmail to write to the Acme client about Sarah's delayed proposal, the Brain's Gmail integration surfaces inside the email compose window — without Maria switching tabs or searching: full Acme commitment history, the risk flag from earlier, Sarah's last recorded status, previous email thread context, and the Q3 revenue goal link. Maria writes a more informed, more credible email in 2 minutes instead of spending 15 minutes hunting through Slack and Salesforce.

name: Evolution
definition: Create organizational learning loops; ensure Brain continuously improves
purpose: Evaluate outcomes; capture lessons; update memory; detect drift
inputs: Actions; Outcomes; Feedback signals; Recommendation outcomes; Exposure outcomes
outputs: Updated organizational memory; Updated learning signals; Policy improvement candidates
plain_english: The Evolution layer closes the organizational learning loop. After every recommendation is accepted or rejected, after every action succeeds or fails, after every piece of intelligence is acted on or ignored, the Evolution layer analyzes those outcomes and asks: what should the Brain learn from this? Validated patterns and lessons update Learning Memory, improving how the Brain reasons about similar situations in the future. This is what makes the Brain get smarter about your specific organization over time — not just AI capability in general, but your organization's particular patterns, failures, and successes.
example: After tracking 10 similar client proposal commitments over 6 months, Evolution detects a pattern: 'Proposal commitments without a recorded pricing approval are 4x more likely to be delayed.' It proposes this as a candidate learning record. After validation (the pattern recurs independently across multiple teams), it is written to Learning Memory. Now, every time a new proposal commitment is created without a pricing approval, the Brain immediately flags it as elevated risk — before any delay occurs.

name: Actor
definition: An entity capable of participating in organizational activity
purpose: Foundation of organizational reality
plain_english: An Actor is anything that can participate in organizational activity — a person, a team, a department, a customer, a vendor, or an AI agent. The concept is intentionally broad: anything that can make commitments, take actions, communicate, or be held accountable is an Actor. Every other primitive either involves Actors (Commitments are between Actors; Communications happen between Actors) or exists to serve them. Without Actors, organizational reality has no participants and no accountability.
example: Sarah (individual employee), the Enterprise Sales Team (team), Acme Corp (external customer), the Legal Department (department), a third-party vendor, a compliance AI agent running automated checks — all are Actors. 'The compliance audit requires sign-off from three Actors: Legal, Finance, and the VP of Operations.' The Brain tracks who is accountable for what by treating every participant — human or AI — as a first-class Actor.

name: Communication
definition: An exchange of meaning between actors
purpose: Foundation of organizational reality
plain_english: A Communication is any exchange of meaning between Actors — anything that carries intent, information, decisions, requests, or feedback from one party to another. It is the raw material from which Commitments are born and Decisions are made. The Brain captures Communications not just as records of what was said, but as the source of organizational understanding — each Communication may contain hidden Commitments, implicit Goals, or contested Rules that the Understanding layer must identify.
example: A Slack message: 'Can you handle the Acme proposal by Thursday?' is a Communication that contains a latent Commitment request. The reply 'Yes, I'll have it done' is a Communication that creates a Commitment. The meeting where both happened is a Communication context. The email with the draft attached is a Communication that may fulfill the Commitment. The Brain treats every one of these as the same primitive type — a Communication — because they all carry meaning between Actors.

name: Commitment
definition: An obligation; responsibility; promise; expectation; or authorization
purpose: Foundation of organizational reality
plain_english: A Commitment is any obligation between Actors — a promise, a task assignment, an expectation, a responsibility, or an authorization to act. This is one of the most critical primitives because most organizational failure happens when commitments are unclear, forgotten, duplicated, or not tracked across their full lifecycle. The Brain treats every Commitment as a living record with an explicit state — not a static note — so it can always answer 'who owes what to whom, and what is the current status?'
example: Sarah says in a meeting: 'I'll send the proposal to Acme by Friday.' That single sentence creates a Commitment: Actor = Sarah, obligated to = Client Team, deliverable = Acme proposal, due = Friday. When Friday passes without a delivery recorded in Action Memory, the Brain does not wait for a human to notice — it automatically updates the Commitment state to Breached and generates an Operational Risk alert. The Commitment was never 'just a note from the meeting.'

name: Action
definition: Work performed that changes organizational state
purpose: Foundation of organizational reality
plain_english: An Action is any work performed that actually changes something in the organization — a process executed, a file delivered, a decision made, a workflow completed, an incident resolved. Actions are what close Commitments and produce outcomes. The Brain carefully distinguishes between intended reality (Commitment: 'I will do X') and actual reality (Action: 'X was done'). The gap between these two — what was promised versus what actually happened — is where most organizational risk and learning live.
example: Sarah sends the proposal email. That is an Action: it creates a record in Action Memory linking back to the original Commitment, marking it Fulfilled, timestamping when it happened, and recording who performed it. If instead of sending the proposal, Sarah updated the deadline (Renegotiated) or handed it to a colleague (Delegated), those would also be Actions — each one changing the state of the Commitment and creating a new organizational reality record.

name: Resource
definition: Something that can be used; consumed; managed; or affected
purpose: Foundation of organizational reality
plain_english: A Resource is anything that can be used, consumed, managed, or affected by organizational activity — money, documents, customer accounts, software systems, time, physical assets, or data. Resources are what Commitments concern ('I will deliver this document') and what Actions act upon ('the document was delivered'). Understanding which Resources are involved in any activity is key to understanding organizational risk, capacity, and dependency — especially when multiple Commitments compete for the same Resource.
example: The Acme proposal document Sarah is creating is a Resource. The client contract is a Resource. The $50k budget that needs CFO approval is a Resource. The shared conference room booked for the client meeting is a Resource. When the Brain detects that two high-priority Commitments both depend on the same engineer's time (a Resource with limited capacity), it can proactively flag a capacity Risk before either commitment falls behind.

name: Rule
definition: A constraint; policy; authority structure; or governing principle
purpose: Foundation of organizational reality
plain_english: A Rule is any constraint, policy, authority structure, or governing principle that defines what is and is not allowed in the organization — approval thresholds, security policies, escalation paths, spending limits, hiring protocols, compliance requirements. Rules are what the Brain's Intelligence layer compares actual Actions against to detect drift and Policy Violations. They define who can approve what, what must happen before something can proceed, and what the organization has formally decided about how it should operate.
example: A policy stating 'All client proposals above $100k require VP approval before sending' is a Rule stored in Factual Memory. A spending limit of $10k per manager is a Rule. An SOP specifying the 8-step customer onboarding process is a Rule. When Action Memory shows a $145k proposal was sent without a VP approval record, the Brain detects a Rule violation and generates a Policy Violation intelligence object — before anyone has to manually audit the paper trail.

name: Goal
definition: A desired future state
purpose: Foundation of organizational reality
plain_english: A Goal is a desired future state — what the organization, a team, or an individual is working toward achieving. Goals give meaning and direction to everything else: they explain why specific Commitments were made, why particular Resources are being used, why certain Rules exist. The Brain uses Goals as the lens through which it evaluates the relevance and urgency of intelligence outputs — a risk only matters in the context of a goal it threatens; an opportunity only matters if there's a goal it serves.
example: Q3 strategic goal: 'Grow enterprise revenue by 20%.' Team goal: 'Launch new platform feature by September 30.' Individual goal for Sarah: 'Close the Acme Corp renewal before Q3 end.' When the Brain generates a Recommendation, it always frames it in the context of an active Goal: 'To achieve Q3 enterprise revenue target, the Acme renewal is currently at high risk due to 3 unresolved commitments and a 60-day engagement gap. Recommended action: executive outreach this week.'

name: State
definition: The current condition of something
purpose: Cross-cutting attribute on every memory record; not a separate store
plain_english: State is the current condition of something — open, in progress, resolved, approved, breached, active, archived, at risk. State is a cross-cutting attribute carried by every memory record across every memory type — not a separate store. The Brain continuously tracks how State changes over time, enabling it to answer time-sensitive questions like 'what is currently at risk?', 'what changed this week?', and 'what commitments are now overdue?' State makes memory dynamic rather than static.
example: A Commitment moves through states: Requested → Promised → Breached (deadline passed). A customer account state transitions: Active → At Risk → Churned. A project moves from: Planning → Executing → On Hold → Cancelled. State is never inferred from context — it is explicitly tracked and updated by the Brain as each relevant event occurs. At any moment, the Brain can answer 'what is the current state of every open commitment?' because State is a first-class attribute of every record.

name: Time
definition: The temporal dimension of organizational activity
purpose: Cross-cutting attribute on every memory record; not a separate store
plain_english: Time is the temporal dimension attached to every organizational event — when something happened, when a Commitment is due, how long something has been open, how recently something was updated. Like State, Time is a cross-cutting attribute carried by every memory record, not a separate store. It enables the Brain to answer time-sensitive questions at scale: 'what's overdue?', 'what's changed since last Monday?', 'how long has this Operational Risk been open without resolution?', 'which commitments have been silent for more than 7 days?'
example: A Commitment is made on Monday with a Friday deadline. The Brain tracks: creation timestamp (Monday 10:04am), due timestamp (Friday 5pm), last-activity timestamp (Monday 10:04am). By Thursday 3pm with no activity recorded, the Brain calculates 94 hours of silence, 26 hours until breach, and surfaces a pre-breach risk alert. This happens automatically — not because someone set a reminder, but because Time is embedded in the Commitment record and the Intelligence layer reads it continuously.

name: Relationship
definition: A meaningful connection between primitives
purpose: Cross-cutting attribute; connective structure across all memory types
plain_english: A Relationship is a meaningful connection between any two primitives — how things are linked together in the organizational reality. Reports-to, depends-on, caused-by, fulfills, authorized-by, created-by, related-to. Without Relationships, the Brain holds isolated facts. With them, it can reason about chains and dependencies: 'this Commitment depends on that Resource which is managed by that Actor who reports to this Manager.' Relationships are what turn a collection of facts into a navigable model of how the organization actually works.
example: Sarah reports-to Maria (Actor–Actor relationship). Sarah's proposal Commitment depends-on the pricing decision (Commitment–Commitment dependency). The pricing decision requires approval from the CFO (Rule–Actor authority relationship). The Acme account is related-to the Q3 revenue Goal. When the Brain surfaces context for a meeting about Acme, it traverses these relationships to show: who's involved, what's at risk, what goals are affected, and whose approval is needed — all from following the relationship graph.

name: Factual Memory
definition: Preserves stable organizational reality
purpose: Store what exists; answer who owns what; what policy governs; what goals are active
inputs: Actors; Resources; Goals; Policies; SOPs; Organizational Structures
plain_english: Factual Memory is the Brain's organizational directory and policy library — the stable, reference-level knowledge about how the organization is structured right now: who works here, what teams exist, what the active goals are, what the approval policies say, what the SOPs define. This is the reference layer that every other reasoning builds on. When something in Factual Memory changes — a team restructures, a policy is updated, a new role is created — the Brain knows to re-evaluate any intelligence that was built on the previous fact.
example: Factual Memory stores: 'Sarah Chen, Senior Account Executive, reports to Maria Lopez, Enterprise Sales Team, US East Region, primary owner of Acme Corp account.' When Maria leaves the company and James takes over as manager, Factual Memory is updated — and the Brain automatically reassigns the ownership context for all open commitments and risks linked to Maria's authority. Without this update, recommendations would reference a manager who no longer exists and approval chains would silently break.

name: Interaction Memory
definition: Preserves organizational reasoning
purpose: Store why decisions were made; what alternatives existed; who objected
plain_english: Interaction Memory is the Brain's record of organizational reasoning — not just what was decided, but why, what alternatives were considered, who disagreed, and what context surrounded the decision. This is the memory type that answers the question every new team member asks: 'why do we do it this way?' It preserves the reasoning behind decisions so it does not die with the people who made them. Without Interaction Memory, organizations lose their institutional reasoning — keeping the outputs but losing the thinking.
example: A critical architectural decision was made in a meeting: 'We chose Vendor A over Vendor B.' Interaction Memory records not just the decision but the full reasoning: 'Vendor B was 20% cheaper but had two security incidents in the last 18 months. Legal and Security both preferred Vendor A. The deciding factor was the multi-year SLA guarantee. Final authority: CTO. Decision confirmed: Vendor A.' When a new engineer joins 8 months later and questions the vendor choice, the Brain can surface the exact reasoning — not a vague summary someone wrote from memory.

name: Commitment Memory
definition: Preserves obligations between actors with full lifecycle tracking
purpose: Track who owes what to whom; what is open; what is overdue
lifecycle: Requested → Promised → Fulfilled / Declined / Delegated / Cancelled / Renegotiated / Breached
plain_english: Commitment Memory is what makes the Brain fundamentally different from a document repository or a note-taking tool. It tracks every promise, task, responsibility, assignment, and obligation across the organization — in real time, with explicit state, at every moment in the commitment lifecycle. It is future-oriented: where most memory describes what happened, Commitment Memory describes what is supposed to happen. This is where 'who owes what to whom, by when, and what is the current status' gets answered with certainty instead of with a search through Slack history.
example: A quarterly planning session generates 34 commitments across 6 teams. Commitment Memory tracks each one: owner, stakeholder, deliverable, deadline, status, and dependencies. By week 3, without anyone asking, it has automatically flagged: 5 commitments as 'Breached' (deadline passed, no completion recorded), 8 as 'At Risk' (no update in 7+ days), 3 as 'Renegotiated' (new timelines agreed), and 2 as 'Delegated' (handoff to another owner). A manager has a complete picture without running a status meeting.

name: Action Memory
definition: Preserves what actually happened
purpose: Store observed execution reality; not intended reality
inputs: Executions; Workflow runs; Incidents; Exceptions; State changes
plain_english: Action Memory is the Brain's record of what actually happened — the executed reality, not the intended one. Every process run, every incident resolved, every workflow completed, every exception handled is recorded in Action Memory. This creates an objective ground truth of how the organization actually operates, which the Intelligence layer continuously compares against intended processes (stored in Factual Memory) to detect drift: the gap between how the organization says it works and how it actually works in practice.
example: The standard customer onboarding process has 8 steps defined in Factual Memory. Action Memory, after 60 completed onboarding cases, reveals that step 5 (security review) was skipped in 42% of cases — not because people are ignoring it intentionally, but because the review request goes to a shared inbox that is frequently missed. No one ran this audit manually. The Brain's Intelligence layer detected the pattern in Action Memory, generated a Drift Signal, and flagged a Process Bottleneck — all without any human intervention.

name: Learning Memory
definition: Preserves organizational learning; primary memory type subject to decay
purpose: Store lessons; patterns; successes; failures; process improvements
inputs: Outcomes; Patterns; Failures; Successes; Drift Analysis
lifecycle: Created → Validated → Used → Reinforced or Decayed → Archived
plain_english: Learning Memory is where the organization's accumulated wisdom lives — validated patterns discovered from outcomes, lessons from failures, successful approaches that worked, process improvements discovered through experience, and heuristics refined over time. Unlike the other memory types which describe reality as it is or was, Learning Memory is prescriptive: it tells the Brain how to reason more accurately about similar situations in the future. It is the organizational equivalent of hard-won experience — except it cannot leave when someone resigns.
example: After tracking three consecutive product launches that all encountered last-minute legal review delays, Learning Memory records a validated pattern: 'Product launches that do not involve Legal from Month 2 onward encounter an average 3–6 week delay in the final month, regardless of team or initiative size. Pattern confirmed across 3 independent instances.' The next time a product launch is planned without Legal in the early schedule, the Brain surfaces this lesson at the moment of planning — before the delay has any chance to materialize.

name: Knowledge Representation
definition: Process by which organizational reality is transformed into canonical knowledge before becoming memory
purpose: Bridge between Understanding layer output and Memory formation
inputs: Primitive Knowledge Objects; Composite Knowledge Objects
outputs: Normalized Knowledge Objects ready for Memory Formation
depends_on: MAIN-KO-001; MAIN-KO-002; MAIN-KO-003; MAIN-KO-004; MAIN-KO-005; MAIN-KO-006; MAIN-KO-007; MAIN-KO-008

name: Memory Formation
definition: Transforms Knowledge Objects into persistent organizational memory via routing; lifecycle management; provenance tracking
purpose: Determine what to remember; which memory type stores it; how to link it; how to preserve provenance
outputs: Routed memory records across five memory types

name: Formation Routing
definition: Determines which memory type(s) a qualifying signal writes to; single event may create records in multiple types
purpose: Route qualified signals to correct memory stores while preserving shared provenance
inputs: Knowledge Objects passing Memory Formation Principle
outputs: Memory records in one or more memory types with shared source reference

name: Memory Lifecycle
definition: All memory records move through defined lifecycle stages; decay and archival are independent processes
purpose: Govern record progression from active to archived; never silently delete
lifecycle: Observed → Interpreted → Recorded → Linked → Used → Updated → Superseded → Archived

name: Provenance
definition: Every memory record carries who asserted it; when; from what source; under which rule version; confidence; challenge status
purpose: Make every memory explainable; answer why we believe this

name: Write Governance
definition: Governs who may create or update memory; AI may propose but not become source of truth
purpose: Ensure memory integrity; control write permissions by actor type

name: Conflict Resolution
definition: Conflicting memories preserved; never silently overwritten; one marked Current one Superseded
purpose: Maintain organizational truth integrity under conflicting evidence
outputs: Current + Superseded record pair with provenance

name: Memory Drift
definition: Detects divergence between intended reality (Policy/SOP) and observed reality (Workflow reconstructed from Action Memory)
purpose: Surface gap between designed and executed process

name: Organizational Learning
definition: Learning occurs when Action Memory patterns produce Learning Memory records that update Policy
purpose: Close learning loop from execution back to governance

name: Memory Consumption & Delivery
definition: Process by which stored memory is assembled; contextualized; and delivered to human or AI actor
purpose: Make memory valuable by delivering it at moment of work
outputs: Context packages; Delivered memory; Feedback signals

name: Context Package Assembly
definition: Assembles distributed memory records into contextualized packages for delivery
purpose: Produce Meeting Brief; Executive Brief; Customer Context; Incident Context etc. from combined memory types
inputs: Factual; Interaction; Commitment; Action; Learning memory records
conflict_flag: resolved — renamed from Context Assembly to distinguish from INT-COMP-001 Reasoning Context Assembly

name: Reasoning Context Assembly
definition: Transforms distributed memory into bounded reasoning context using relevance; recency; goal linkage; actor proximity; commitment linkage
purpose: Produce context package ready for reasoning pipeline
inputs: All five memory types; Current Actor; Current Goal; Current Query; Current Constraints
conflict_flag: resolved — renamed from Context Assembly; receives Context Package from MEM-COMP-010; sequential not duplicate

name: Reasoning Pipeline
definition: Transforms Context into Intelligence through staged evaluation; branches per Consultant mode
purpose: Core reasoning engine of Intelligence layer
lifecycle: Situation Understanding → Goal Evaluation → Constraint Evaluation → Commitment Evaluation → Risk Evaluation → Opportunity Evaluation → Recommendation Generation

name: Recommendation Intelligence
definition: Generates actionable guidance with reasoning; confidence; and sources
purpose: Produce why-backed recommendations from context; goals; rules; commitments; learning

name: Risk Intelligence
definition: Detects possible future conditions threatening goals; commitments; resources; or organizational health
purpose: Surface operational risks before they materialize
inputs: Open Commitments; Historical Failures; Policy Violations; Resource Constraints; Drift Signals

name: Opportunity Intelligence
definition: Detects possible future conditions increasing value; efficiency; alignment; or goal achievement
purpose: Surface potential value before it is lost
inputs: Success Patterns; Customer Signals; Resource Availability; Relationship Signals; Learning Memory

name: Drift Intelligence
definition: Detects divergence between intended reality (Policy/SOP) and observed reality (Workflow); three-stage escalation to confirmed Drift Signal
purpose: Surface policy-practice gap with evidence threshold
inputs: Policy; SOP; Workflow; Action Memory patterns
lifecycle: Drift Candidate → Drift Pattern → Drift Signal

name: Consultant Intelligence
definition: Intelligence consumer operating in four modes; each with distinct pipeline branching behavior
purpose: Power Consultant product surface across Inquiry; Planning; Review; Simulation
outputs: Mode-specific outputs: explanation / recommendations / progress report / scenario comparisons
lifecycle: Inquiry → Evidence-based explanation; Planning → Full pipeline → Recommendations; Review → Progress & Risk Report; Simulation → Scenario Comparisons

name: Agent Intelligence
definition: Converts intelligence into execution plans; assesses Agent Readiness; escalates when confidence below threshold
purpose: Enable agents to act autonomously with appropriate human handoff
inputs: Intelligence outputs; Agent goals; Permissions; Confidence scores
outputs: Execution plans; Agent Readiness assessments; Escalations

name: Confidence Model
definition: Conceptual five-level confidence assessment driven by evidence strength; source quality; agreement; freshness; completeness; with asymmetric behavior by output type
purpose: Govern how intelligence outputs behave at each confidence level; prevent false certainty
inputs: Evidence; Source quality; Agreement across memories; Freshness; Completeness
outputs: Confidence level per intelligence object; Behavioral directive
lifecycle: Very Low → Low → Medium → High → Very High

name: Adaptive Intelligence
definition: Improves reasoning over time via repeated validated feedback; writes back only through Memory Model Write Governance; single feedback never equals learning
purpose: Prevent reasoning stagnation without self-corruption on noisy signals
outputs: Learning Memory candidates proposed to MEM-COMP-005
lifecycle: Observation → Single Feedback (not learning) → Repeated Validated Feedback → Learning Memory candidate → Write Governance

name: Intelligence Object Freshness & Decay
definition: Confidence decays on active intelligence objects as supporting evidence ages; decay ≠ resolution; terminal-state objects retain historical confidence
purpose: Prevent stale intelligence from being presented at original confidence indefinitely
inputs: Active intelligence objects; Evidence age; Organizational context changes
consumed_by: INT-OBJ-001; INT-OBJ-002; INT-OBJ-003; INT-OBJ-004; INT-OBJ-005; INT-OBJ-006; INT-OBJ-007; INT-OBJ-008; INT-OBJ-009; INT-OBJ-010
lifecycle: Active states only — decay stops at terminal state

name: Recommendation
definition: Suggested action with reasoning; confidence; and sources
purpose: Turn intelligence into actionable guidance
owner: Actor or team recommendation is directed at
plain_english: A Recommendation is the Brain's most direct output: here is what you should do, here is why, and here is who should act on it. It is the result of the full reasoning pipeline — context assembled from all memory stores, goals evaluated, constraints checked, risks weighed — distilled into an actionable suggestion with the reasoning and sources attached. Every Recommendation has an owner (the specific person or team who should act), a confidence level, and a lifecycle: it does not disappear once generated. It stays open until someone accepts it, rejects it, or modifies it — and the Brain tracks what happened to it.
example: Brain reasoning context: Acme Corp renewal is in 45 days. Last 3 support tickets are unresolved (Action Memory). Executive sponsor contact has not been engaged in 60 days (Interaction Memory). Commitment from Q2 review: 'schedule quarterly executive check-in' — still status Promised, never fulfilled (Commitment Memory). Q3 revenue goal: $2.4M (Factual Memory). Recommendation generated: 'Schedule executive check-in with Acme Corp this week. Renewal at high risk — unresolved support issues and 60-day engagement gap detected. Owner: Maria Lopez (Account Manager). Confidence: High. Review Trigger: Acme meeting scheduled.'

name: Operational Risk
definition: Detected future threat to goals; commitments; resources; or organizational health; not withheld at low confidence — tracked with unconfirmed flag
purpose: Surface threats early even at low confidence
plain_english: An Operational Risk is the Brain's detection of a possible future threat to goals, commitments, resources, or organizational health. Unlike a Recommendation (which says 'do this to achieve something positive'), a Risk says 'be aware — something may go wrong.' Critically, Operational Risks are never suppressed even at low confidence: it is better to surface an unconfirmed risk with a 'low confidence / unconfirmed' flag than to miss a real threat. Risks remain open until genuinely resolved — confidence may decay over time, but the risk itself stays visible until closed.
example: Intelligence analysis: three senior engineers are assigned to the same critical infrastructure release (Factual Memory). Action Memory shows all three are at 90%+ capacity utilization this sprint. Commitment Memory shows two of their key dependencies are in 'Blocked' status with no resolution timeline. Operational Risk generated: 'Release INFRA-2024-Q3 at capacity and dependency risk. Three key engineers near full utilization with two blocked dependencies. Owner: Engineering Lead James. Confidence: High. Severity: High. Review Trigger: Dependency Status Change.' Risk stays open until both blocked items resolve.

name: Opportunity Signal
definition: Pattern-detected hint that potential value exists; becomes Opportunity ontology object only once resources committed
purpose: Surface value before formal commitment
owner: Team or role positioned to act
plain_english: An Opportunity Signal is the Brain detecting a possible future positive — a chance to create value, increase efficiency, improve goal alignment, or accelerate achievement. It is the optimistic counterpart to Operational Risk. The Brain generates Opportunity Signals by recognizing patterns in Learning Memory (what has worked before), noticing available Resources, detecting positive relationship signals, and identifying favorable timing windows — then surfacing them while the window is still open, not after it has closed.
example: Learning Memory has a validated pattern: 'When enterprise RFP responses are submitted within 48 hours of receipt, win rate is 3.1x higher than the average, confirmed across 14 independent cases.' A new high-value RFP has just arrived from a target-sector enterprise prospect (detected via email capture). Opportunity Signal generated: 'High-value RFP received from priority enterprise prospect. Historical pattern: responding within 48 hours increases win rate 3x. Current time since receipt: 4 hours. Assign proposal lead immediately. Owner: Sales Lead. Confidence: High. Review Trigger: 24 hours elapsed.'

name: Drift Signal
definition: Confirmed divergence between intended and observed reality; requires confidence ≥ Medium per Confidence Model
purpose: Surface policy-practice gap with sufficient evidence
plain_english: A Drift Signal is the Brain detecting that how the organization actually operates has diverged from how it is supposed to operate — a gap between the intended and the observed. The Brain continuously compares Action Memory (what actually happened) against the Rules and SOPs in Factual Memory (what was supposed to happen). A single divergence is a Drift Candidate. A repeated pattern of divergence, confirmed across multiple independent instances, becomes a Drift Signal — hard evidence that a structural process gap exists. This is how the Brain detects the gap between the organization on paper and the organization in practice.
example: Company policy (Factual Memory): all client proposals require pricing approval before sending (Rule). Action Memory analysis over 90 days: 6 of 18 proposals were sent without a recorded pricing approval event. Pattern confirmed across 3 different account executives, 2 different regions. Drift Signal generated: 'Pricing approval step bypassed in 33% of proposal processes. Policy defines it as mandatory. Observed behavior: inconsistent. Severity: Medium. Owner: Sales Operations Lead. Lifecycle: Detected → Confirmed (pattern threshold met) → Investigating. Review Trigger: Process Execution Change.'

name: Knowledge Gap
definition: Missing organizational understanding detected by reasoning
purpose: Surface where Brain lacks sufficient knowledge to reason reliably
plain_english: A Knowledge Gap is the Brain recognizing that it does not know something it should know — that there is missing organizational understanding which creates risk, limits decision quality, or blocks execution. This might be a key contact whose decision authority is unknown, a project with no documented owner, a process that exists in practice but has never been formally captured, or a commitment whose resolution was never recorded. Knowledge Gaps are actionable: they identify a specific gap and assign someone responsibility for closing it.
example: A new enterprise deal moves to contract stage and requires understanding the client's procurement process and approval authority. Brain searches all memory stores: no procurement contact recorded for this client, no process documentation exists, no prior contract history with this contact, no interaction records about their procurement timeline. Knowledge Gap generated: 'Acme Corp procurement process and approval authority unknown. This gap creates risk for contract timeline — average contract delay from unknown procurement is 3–5 weeks. Owner: Account Executive Sarah. Required action: establish procurement contact and document process within 5 business days. Confidence impact: High.'

name: Prediction
definition: Forecast of a future organizational state
purpose: Enable proactive planning and risk awareness
plain_english: A Prediction is the Brain's probabilistic forecast of a future organizational state — not a certainty, but an evidence-based projection based on historical patterns from Learning Memory, current trajectories from Action Memory, and active commitments from Commitment Memory. Predictions are how the Brain operates in simulation mode: given what we know now and what has historically happened in similar circumstances, here is what is likely to happen. They have a full lifecycle — generated, tracked as reality evolves, and ultimately confirmed or falsified, either outcome becoming learning.
example: Sprint SPRINT-22 has 9 tasks. Current completion rate: 4 tasks closed with 3 days remaining. Two open blockers are unresolved (Commitment Memory). Learning Memory has a pattern: 'Sprints at 44% completion with 3 days left and ≥2 blockers historically close at 60–68% capacity.' Prediction generated: 'Sprint SPRINT-22 projected to complete at approximately 65% (6 of 9 tasks). Current trajectory: 3 tasks likely to carry over. Recommended action: defer 3 lowest-priority tasks before Friday to protect team focus. Confidence: Medium. Review Trigger: Sprint closure or blocker resolution.'

name: Policy Violation
definition: Observed breach of defined Policy or Rule
purpose: Surface compliance failures for resolution or formal exception
plain_english: A Policy Violation is the Brain detecting a concrete, specific, already-occurred breach of a defined Rule — not a risk of future violation (that would be Operational Risk), not a pattern of drift (that is Drift Signal), but a specific identifiable instance where a Rule was not followed. The difference matters for governance: Violations have an explicit owner (typically the Policy owner or relevant authority), a tracked lifecycle, and a formal resolution path — either the violation is corrected, or it is formally closed via an approved Exception acknowledging the deviation.
example: Rule in Factual Memory: 'No contract above $100k may be executed without CFO signature. CFO = David Kim.' Action Memory records: Contract C-2024-089, value $145,000, marked as Executed. Approval records for C-2024-089 in Commitment Memory: shows only VP Finance signature, no CFO signature recorded. Policy Violation generated: 'Contract C-2024-089 ($145k) executed without CFO signature. Policy mandates CFO approval on contracts above $100k. Owner: CFO Office. Lifecycle: Detected → Validated (confirmed by reviewing approval records) → Escalated to CFO David Kim for review. Resolution: Correct retroactively or formally Exception.'

name: Process Bottleneck
definition: Recurring constraint slowing execution detected from Action Memory patterns
purpose: Surface systemic execution friction
plain_english: A Process Bottleneck is the Brain identifying a recurring structural constraint that is systematically slowing execution — not a one-time delay or an individual performance issue, but a repeating pattern where a specific step in a process consistently fails to meet its intended timing. The Brain detects these by analyzing Action Memory at scale across many instances of the same process type, asking: where do commitments and workflows consistently get stuck? Where does the same step repeatedly exceed expected time? Where do the same exceptions repeatedly occur?
example: Action Memory analysis across 60 completed customer onboarding cases: the 'Legal contract review' step has a median completion time of 11 days against the 3-day SOP target. This occurs in 82% of cases with no apparent relationship to contract complexity or customer type — it is structural, not case-by-case. Process Bottleneck generated: 'Legal contract review is completing in 3.7x the SOP target time in 82% of onboarding cases. This adds an average 8-day delay to customer go-live. Root cause: likely capacity or intake process. Owner: Legal Team Lead. Priority: High. Review Trigger: Workflow Execution Change.'

name: Agent Readiness
definition: Assessment of agent fitness to act autonomously on given action class; driven by same Confidence Model as all intelligence objects
purpose: Gate autonomous agent execution; trigger escalation when below threshold
conflict_flag: no — two-axis pairing with TRU-COMP-008; Readiness=Intelligence; Authority=Trust per T&G §9
plain_english: Agent Readiness is the Brain's formal assessment of whether an AI agent has sufficient context, adequate confidence, and the required clarity to execute a specific action autonomously — or whether it must escalate to a human. This is a safety gate that runs before any agent acts: does the agent know enough, and is it confident enough, to proceed without human input? Agent Readiness is distinct from Agent Authority (which asks 'is the agent allowed to act at all?') — both must pass before execution. Failing Readiness triggers escalation; failing Authority triggers a hard block.
example: An agent is tasked with sending a contract renewal to Acme Corp. Agent Readiness assessment: contract value $75k (within scope), pricing has a recorded Approval in Commitment Memory, legal review is Completed in Action Memory, contact email is verified in Factual Memory. Readiness assessment: Certified — proceed. But if the legal review were missing (no Action Memory record of completion), Readiness assessment: Not Ready — escalate to Account Executive Sarah before sending. The agent reports what is missing and waits for human clearance. It does not proceed on assumption.

name: Brain Score
definition: Aggregate health metric computed by rolling up confidence; drift severity; unresolved risk across a scope; not event-driven
purpose: Provide organizational health visibility at team/project/org level
inputs: Confidence levels; Drift severity; Unresolved risk counts
lifecycle: Calculated → Published → Recalculated on material change
plain_english: Brain Score is the Brain's aggregate organizational health metric — a composite indicator that rolls up confidence levels across active intelligence objects, drift severity, unresolved Operational Risks, and commitment fulfillment rates into a single score for a defined organizational scope: a team, a project, a business unit, or the whole organization. It is not a vanity metric or a dashboard decoration — it is a real-time signal of how well the organization is operating against its commitments and goals, updated continuously as the underlying reality changes.
example: Q3 Acme Migration Project Brain Score: 58/100 (Declined from 74 last month). Contributing factors: 3 open Operational Risks (1 Critical, 2 High), 1 active Drift Signal (approval step being bypassed), commitment fulfillment rate 68% against 85% target, 2 Knowledge Gaps unresolved, 1 Policy Violation under investigation. The score is surfaced automatically on the Project Sponsor's Personal Reality view every morning. Trend: declining. A score change of more than 10 points triggers a Recommendation to the project owner to initiate a formal review.

name: Claim
definition: Memory record or Intelligence Object assertion viewed through trust lens; carries Trust Lifecycle
purpose: Unit of trust assessment across all memory and intelligence outputs
plain_english: A Claim is any assertion in the Brain's memory or intelligence viewed through a trust lens — it is the unit of 'this is something we believe to be true.' Every fact in Factual Memory, every Recommendation from Intelligence, every decision recorded in Interaction Memory is technically a Claim that carries a trust state. The Trust system manages how that state evolves: has it been verified? Has someone challenged it? Has new evidence strengthened or weakened it? Claims are not just stored — they are continuously governed through a trust lifecycle.
example: 'Sarah Chen is the primary owner of the Acme Corp account' is a Claim in Factual Memory. It starts as Asserted (loaded from CRM data). After a manager confirms it in onboarding, it moves to Verified. After months of consistent behavior and no challenges, it becomes Trusted. When Sarah is promoted and a new AE takes over Acme but the handover is informal, someone Challenges the Claim. Brain moves it to Challenged status — reduces confidence in Acme-related Recommendations, flags it for resolution — and it stays Challenged until a human formally revalidates the ownership.

name: Evidence
definition: Sources field on every memory record and intelligence object; this doc defines who may submit and what authority required
purpose: Establish basis for trusting a Claim
inputs: Memory provenance fields; Intelligence source fields
plain_english: Evidence is what makes a Claim trustworthy — the specific sources, records, and supporting information that back up an assertion. The Trust system does not create a separate evidence database; Evidence is the Sources field that already exists on every Memory record and Intelligence Object, now governed: who may submit it, what authority is required for it to count toward verifying a Claim, and whether the volume and quality of Evidence is sufficient to move a Claim from Asserted to Verified. A Claim without Evidence is an unverified assertion; Evidence is what transforms assertion into trust.
example: 'Q3 revenue target is $2.4M' is a Claim. Evidence: board-approved Q3 plan (uploaded to Factual Memory, source: CFO, date: April 3rd — high authority, primary source), sales forecast from Salesforce (CRM sync, date: April 5th — secondary confirmation). Two independent authoritative sources. Evidence: Strong. Claim moves from Asserted to Verified to Trusted. If only the CRM forecast existed with no board document, Evidence would be: Insufficient — Claim stays at Asserted. Intelligence objects built on this Claim would carry a lower confidence flag.

name: Challenge
definition: Formal dispute against a Claim; distinct from Conflict Resolution which handles contradicting records
purpose: Enable any authorized actor to dispute organizational truth
plain_english: A Challenge is a formal dispute against a Claim — when an Actor with standing believes an assertion in the Brain is wrong, outdated, incomplete, or insufficiently evidenced. Challenge is distinct from Conflict Resolution (which automatically handles contradicting records from different sources) — Challenge handles human-initiated disputes of specific claims. It requires standing to raise and authority to resolve, and it is not optional: the Trust architecture requires that any organizational truth can be challenged. No fact in the Brain is beyond dispute.
example: 'Vendor contract renewal date is December 15th' is a Claim in Factual Memory, sourced from an internal calendar reminder. The Procurement team Challenges this: their vendor portal shows November 30th as the actual renewal date. Challenge Raised → Legal Team Assigned to Review → Evidence examined: vendor portal screenshot (stronger source than internal calendar) → Challenge Accepted. Original Claim marked Superseded. New Claim with corrected date: Verified. Full audit trail preserved: who challenged, when, what evidence decided it, and who held resolution authority.

name: Approval
definition: Authorization event instantiated per context; Write Governance tier; Three-Tier Boundary gate; Adaptive Learning approval; governed by one authority model
purpose: Authorize memory writes; agent actions; policy changes; learning updates
inputs: Authorization request; Reviewing actor; Authority check
plain_english: An Approval is a formal authorization event — a recorded instance where someone with the appropriate authority reviewed something and authorized it to proceed. The Trust system governs Approvals consistently across every context where they appear in the Brain: a new memory write, an agent taking an action, a policy exception being granted, a learning update being applied. All of these use the same Approval lifecycle — Requested → Reviewed → Approved or Rejected → Executed — creating a uniform, auditable authorization record throughout the Brain regardless of what is being approved.
example: An AI agent proposes adding a new learning pattern to Memory: 'Enterprise proposals without a recorded pricing approval have a 4x higher breach rate.' Before any write occurs, an Approval is required per Write Governance rules. Approval lifecycle begins: Requested (agent submits proposal to Memory governance queue) → Reviewed (Sales Operations Lead reviews the pattern's evidence — 14 instances across 90 days) → Approved (Sales Ops Lead authorizes the write) → Executed (Memory Model's Write Governance records the pattern). Full audit trail: agent proposed, Sales Ops Lead approved at 2:14pm on June 15th, under Sales Operations ownership authority.

name: Exception
definition: Formally approved deviation; resolution path for open Policy Violation or Drift Signal when divergence accepted rather than corrected
purpose: Close Policy Violation or Drift Signal via acceptance rather than fix
inputs: Policy Violation or Drift Signal; Approval; Reviewing actor
lifecycle: Proposed → Reviewed → Approved → Active → Expired / Revoked
plain_english: An Exception is a formally approved deviation from a Rule or Policy — an explicit, documented record that the organization has consciously decided to allow a specific departure from its normal operating rules, for a specific reason, for a defined period. Exceptions are the proper resolution path for Policy Violations and Drift Signals when the right response is 'this deviation is accepted' rather than 'this deviation must be corrected.' They are bounded: Exceptions expire or can be revoked, and when they do, normal policy enforcement automatically restores.
example: Policy: no software may go to production without a completed security review (Factual Memory). A critical bug is causing a data display error for 200 enterprise customers — a fix is ready in 2 hours, but a full security review takes 48 hours. Exception: Proposed (by Engineering Lead) → Reviewed (CISO evaluates: patch is 3 files, no authentication changes, low attack surface) → Approved (CISO grants, conditions: limited to specific files, security review required within 48 hours) → Active. The Policy Violation that would have been generated is closed via Exception — not as Resolved-as-fixed, accurately reflecting what actually occurred. Exception expires at 48 hours. Policy enforcement restores automatically.

name: Escalation
definition: Request to raise authority; defines authority chain that Intelligence confidence-based and readiness-based triggers invoke
purpose: Route decisions to appropriate authority level when current actor lacks sufficient authority
plain_english: An Escalation is a formal request to raise authority — to involve a higher-level decision-maker because the current actor's authority is insufficient for the action or decision at hand. Escalations are not just notifications or informal messages; they have a governed lifecycle and a defined authority chain. The Intelligence layer determines when to escalate based on confidence thresholds and Readiness assessments. The Trust system defines to whom the escalation goes and with what standing. This ensures that decisions are made at the correct authority level, and that the escalation itself is tracked and resolved — not left open.
example: An agent is processing a contract renewal at $85,000. Agent Readiness: Certified (full context available, confidence High). Agent Authority check: $85k exceeds the automated VP-level approval limit of $50k. Escalation triggered: Requested (by agent, with full context package attached) → Assigned (to CFO David Kim, per authority chain: VP threshold exceeded → CFO required) → Reviewed (CFO reviews contract, pricing, and risk summary) → Resolved (CFO approves; agent receives clearance and proceeds). The agent never bypasses the authority chain even though it is confident the renewal is straightforward — confidence is Agent Readiness; authority is Trust Governance.

name: Delegation
definition: Transfer of existing authority from one actor to another; delegation never creates authority only redistributes it
purpose: Enable flexible authority distribution while preserving traceability
inputs: Granting actor; Receiving actor; Authority scope; Policy constraints
plain_english: A Delegation is a formal transfer of existing authority from one Actor to another — with a full lifecycle, explicit scope, and the hard constraint that you can never delegate more authority than you currently possess. Delegations are traceable: the Brain maintains a complete chain of who delegated to whom, when, under what conditions, and what scope was transferred. They are time-bounded and revocable: when a Delegation expires or is revoked, the authority automatically returns to the granting actor. This prevents authority from accumulating through cascading delegations without clear accountability.
example: Maria (VP Sales) is going on three weeks of parental leave. She delegates her deal approval authority — up to $50k — to James (Senior Account Executive). Delegation created: Active. While active, James can approve deals up to $50k. James cannot approve $75k deals (even if he has high conviction) because he only received $50k of delegated authority — Delegation cannot create authority that did not exist. When Maria returns and formally revokes the Delegation: Active → Revoked → Authority Returns To Maria. James's approval authority immediately returns to his standard limit. Audit trail: Maria delegated on June 1st under VP Sales authority, revoked June 22nd, full chain traceable.

name: Provenance Architecture
definition: Every significant object across Memory; Intelligence; Execution must answer who; what; when; why; under what authority; does not redefine Memory or Intelligence provenance fields
purpose: Unify provenance requirements across all layers

name: Authority Model
definition: Defines authority sources (Role; Ownership; Policy; Delegation; Approval) built on Ontology Person/Team/Role objects; answers who can write; approve; challenge; delegate
purpose: Single authority source for all governance decisions
consumed_by: TRU-COMP-003; TRU-COMP-004; TRU-COMP-005; TRU-COMP-006; TRU-COMP-007; TRU-COMP-008; TRU-COMP-009
plain_english: The Authority Model is the framework that answers 'who is allowed to do what, and on what basis?' It defines the five sources from which authority flows in the Brain: Role (authority attached to a position), Ownership (authority over what you own), Policy (authority defined by organizational rules), Delegation (authority transferred from another actor), and Approval (authority granted through a formal authorization event). Every governance decision in the Brain — who can write to memory, who can approve an agent action, who can validate a learning candidate — traces back to one of these five sources, making authority legible and auditable rather than tribal.
example: A new learning candidate needs approval: 'Enterprise proposals without pricing approval have 4x higher breach rates.' Who has authority to approve this? Authority Model traversal: what is this? → A write to Learning Memory concerning proposal processes. Who owns proposal processes? → Sales Operations (Ownership source). Who is the Sales Operations Lead? → Fatima Hassan. Therefore: Fatima Hassan has authority to approve this learning write under the Ownership source. The Brain does not need to look up a permissions table — it traverses the Authority Model to determine the correct approver. No tribal knowledge required.

name: Delegation Boundary Principle
definition: Delegation transfers authority but never creates it; delegated authority may never exceed original grant; chains must remain traceable
purpose: Prevent authority escalation through delegation
plain_english: The Delegation Boundary Principle is the foundational rule of authority transfer in the Brain: delegation redistributes authority, it does not create it. You can give someone authority you possess; you cannot give someone authority you do not have. Every delegation chain must remain fully traceable — you must always be able to trace 'who originally held this authority, through what sequence of delegations did it reach the current holder, and does each link remain valid?' This prevents authority inflation, where cascading delegations could create more permission than anyone originally intended to grant.
example: Authority chain: CEO holds $5M approval authority → delegates $1M to CFO → CFO delegates $500k to VP Finance → VP Finance attempts to delegate $600k to the Finance Director. The Delegation Boundary Principle blocks the last step: VP Finance only holds $500k of delegated authority, so the maximum they can delegate forward is $500k. The Finance Director receives at most $500k. Chain: CEO ($5M) → CFO ($1M) → VP Finance ($500k) → Director ($500k). Every link is traceable. The principle prevents the Director from ever possessing $600k authority through this chain regardless of how the request is framed.

name: Revocation Principle
definition: Any delegated authority; Approval; or Exception may be revoked by actor of equal or greater authority than granting actor
purpose: Ensure authority can contract as well as expand
inputs: TRU-OBJ-004; TRU-OBJ-005; TRU-OBJ-007; Revoking actor authority
plain_english: The Revocation Principle establishes that authority is not permanent — any Approval, Exception, or Delegation may be withdrawn by an Actor who holds equal or greater authority than the one who originally granted it. This is the governance system's correction mechanism: if a delegation was made in error, if an exception should no longer apply, if an approval was premature, or if organizational circumstances change — all of these can be formally reversed. Critically, revocation is not silent: the Brain records the revocation with its reason, timestamp, and authority, creating a complete governance audit trail of what was granted and what was taken back.
example: A manager granted a team lead an Exception allowing them to bypass the standard purchase approval process for items under $5,000. The company is acquired and the parent company's financial controls require all purchases above $1,000 to be approved. The CFO (higher authority than the manager who granted the Exception) revokes it. Revocation: Exception state moves Active → Revoked → Policy Enforcement Restored. The team lead immediately loses the bypass capability. The Brain records: Exception granted by Manager A on January 15th, revoked by CFO on June 1st (authority: higher organizational authority, trigger: policy change). Every future purchase follows standard approval.

name: Trust Failure Principle
definition: When trust requirements unmet system discloses uncertainty; limits automation; escalates authority; requests human review; trust overrides autonomy
purpose: Prevent system from hiding uncertainty; reduce autonomy not increase risk on trust failure

plain_english: The Trust Failure Principle defines what the Brain does when trust requirements cannot be satisfied — and the answer is always: surface the problem, never hide it. When trust conditions fail (missing provenance, conflicting authority, unresolved Challenge, insufficient Evidence, expired Approval), the Brain follows a strict four-step response: disclose the uncertainty explicitly, limit automation to prevent unsafe autonomous action, escalate to higher authority, and request human review. The principle's core rule: trust always overrides autonomy. An agent may be capable and Ready. If Trust requirements are not met, it does not proceed.
example: An agent is about to deliver a strategic recommendation to a customer about Q4 investment priorities. Trust check on the underlying risk assessment: there is an unresolved Challenge (a senior analyst disputed the revenue projection data 4 days ago — still open). Trust failure condition: unresolved Challenge on supporting Claim. Trust Failure behavior activates: Disclose Uncertainty (recommendation now shows 'Confidence: Low — underlying data under review by Analyst Team') → Limit Automation (agent blocked from auto-delivering) → Escalate (Account Executive Sarah notified with full context) → Request Human Review (Sarah must manually review and decide whether to send, modify, or hold). Agent was Ready. Trust was not met. Trust wins.

name: Ambient Delivery

plain_english: Ambient Delivery is the Brain's primary delivery mode for most users — and the key insight is that users never have to open a separate application. The Brain comes to the user wherever work is already happening: inside Gmail as they compose an email, in a Slack thread as a message is read, in a calendar view before a meeting starts, in a CRM account page as a record is reviewed. It surfaces relevant organizational memory contextually and at the right moment, without interrupting flow, without requiring a search, and without demanding that users change their behavior.
example: Maria is writing an email to the Acme Corp CTO about their upcoming contract renewal. Without switching tabs or opening a separate tool, the Brain surfaces inside Gmail: '3 open commitments linked to this contact — 1 is overdue (proposal from Sarah, due June 14th). 2 previous emails referenced a pricing concern that was flagged but never formally resolved. Decision recorded April 23rd: VP approved custom pricing exception for Acme.' Maria has the complete context before hitting send — not because she searched for it, but because the Brain knew she needed it at exactly this moment.

name: Agent Access

plain_english: Agent Access is how AI systems — external tools like Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, Windsurf — access the Brain's organizational memory and intelligence directly. The Brain acts as an MCP (Model Context Protocol) provider: any AI tool that supports MCP can query the Brain and receive organizational context, commitment histories, risk signals, and knowledge objects. This transforms the Brain from a human-facing interface into organizational memory infrastructure that any AI reasoning system can tap into — making every AI tool your team uses inherently context-aware about your organization.
example: A sales engineer opens Cursor to draft a technical proposal for a new enterprise prospect. Without copying anything into the prompt, the Brain automatically provides Cursor with: the prospect's industry and known technical requirements (Factual Memory), a similar proposal that won a comparable deal 6 months ago (Learning Memory), two open commitments the team made to the prospect during initial discovery calls (Commitment Memory), and a risk flag that their procurement lead prefers shorter proposal formats (Interaction Memory). The engineer's AI-assisted draft starts from full organizational context — not from a blank page.

purpose: Provide deep understanding and control when required

outputs: Investigation views; Governance actions; Coordination surfaces
plain_english: Mission Control is the dedicated workspace you navigate to when ambient context is not enough — when you need to investigate, govern, oversee, coordinate, or understand something in depth. It is not the primary interface for most users on most days (Ambient Delivery handles day-to-day context). Mission Control is where managers, executives, and operators go to work actively with organizational memory: reviewing the real state of commitments across a team, investigating a risk, overseeing agent activity, or understanding what is happening across multiple initiatives at once.
example: The COO wants to understand the actual state of Q3 strategic initiatives before a board call. She opens Mission Control → Operational Intelligence. In 10 minutes she sees: 6 open Operational Risks across 3 initiatives (2 Critical, 4 High), 2 active Drift Signals on core processes, 12 commitments marked Breached with no resolution in progress, one declining Brain Score on the Migration project (dropped from 74 to 58 this month). She can drill into any item, see the full evidence chain, and walk into the board call with the actual picture — not a status report someone assembled from memory.

name: Personal Reality

purpose: Turn memory into daily operational clarity
plain_english: Personal Reality is an individual's Mission Control view — the Brain's answer to 'what should I personally be paying attention to right now?' It aggregates everything relevant to one person: their open Commitments, items that are overdue, Recommendations directed at them, decisions that affect their work, suggested actions, and the team context most relevant to their current role. The goal is to let every person start their day with a complete, accurate picture of what requires their attention — without assembling it manually from Slack, email, project tools, and their own memory.
example: Monday morning, 8:47am. Sarah opens Personal Reality: 'Open commitments: 4 (1 Breached — Acme proposal, due June 14th; 2 Promised — within timeline; 1 Requested — needs your acceptance). Recommendations directed at you: 1 (Schedule executive check-in with Acme Corp — renewal risk high). Decisions affecting you: Maria approved budget increase for Q3 enterprise accounts — review scope. Team context: Maria on leave until Wednesday (James is covering deal approvals). Intelligence: Acme account Brain Score declined to 58 this week.' Sarah knows exactly where to start without checking 5 different tools.

name: Team Reality
definition: Shows team commitments; risks; blockers; dependencies; capacity; drift signals
purpose: Turn organizational memory into team awareness
plain_english: Team Reality is the Mission Control view for managers and team leads — the Brain's answer to 'how is my team actually performing right now, based on what is really happening rather than what was reported?' It aggregates commitment fulfillment rates, open risks, blockers, capacity signals, and drift indicators across the entire team. This gives managers an objective, continuously updated picture of team health — grounded in Action Memory and Commitment Memory — rather than relying on status meetings, self-reported updates, or whatever surfaces in Slack.
example: Wednesday afternoon. Engineering Manager reviews Team Reality: 'Sprint SPRINT-22: 61% complete with 3 days remaining (target: 75%+ by Wednesday). Capacity: 2 engineers at 95%+ utilization (flagged). Open blockers: 1 Process Bottleneck on code review step (taking 3x normal time). Drift Signal: deployment checklist bypassed in 4 of the last 10 deployments. Team commitments: 8 open, 2 Breached, 3 At Risk.' This is more accurate than last Friday's status report because it reflects what has actually happened in the last 72 hours — not what people remembered to update.

definition: Multi-channel feed of what changed that matters; commitments; decisions; policy updates; drift signals; agent approvals; learning events; conflicts
purpose: Reduce organizational forgetting; deliver change awareness
outputs: Feed items across Dashboard; Slack; Email; Browser; Mobile
plain_english: Reality Feed is the Brain's curated, real-time event stream — a live view of organizationally significant things happening right now, filtered to what is relevant to you, your team, and your goals. Unlike a generic notification feed that shows every activity regardless of importance, Reality Feed is filtered by the Intelligence layer: only events that cross a relevance threshold for the viewer appear. It shows commitment status changes, new risk detections, Brain Score movements, learning updates, and intelligence object state changes as they happen in real time.
example: Reality Feed updates in one morning: 09:04 — 'Acme Corp commitment COMM-089 status changed: Promised → Breached (Sarah Chen, owner. No activity for 8 days).' 09:41 — 'New Operational Risk detected on Project Mercury: capacity constraint, 3 engineers at 90%+ utilization.' 10:17 — 'Q3 revenue Brain Score declined: 74 → 68 (two new Operational Risks added this week).' 11:02 — 'Learning Memory updated: new pattern validated — cross-functional proposals without Legal from Month 2 delay by avg 4.2 weeks.' Each entry is clickable and opens the full evidence and context.

name: Organizational Memory
definition: Search; Timeline; Relationship Graph; Provenance; History — answers why questions about organizational decisions and commitments
purpose: Turn memory into organizational understanding
outputs: Search results; Timeline view; Relationship graph; Provenance view
plain_english: Organizational Memory is Mission Control's deliberate search and exploration surface — the interface for querying the Brain's full knowledge base when you have a specific question and need to go find the answer. Where Reality Feed shows you what is happening now, and Personal Reality shows what needs your attention, Organizational Memory lets you search and navigate across all five memory types to reconstruct the past, understand context, and trace the history of decisions, commitments, and outcomes. It is the Brain's library — structured, searchable, fully traceable to source documents.
example: A new Product Manager joins and wants to understand why the team uses the current database architecture instead of the alternative they considered. She searches Organizational Memory: 'database architecture decision 2023.' Interaction Memory returns the decision record from a meeting 14 months ago: 7 attendees listed, 3 alternatives considered (PostgreSQL, MongoDB, CockroachDB), the specific concerns raised about MongoDB's consistency model at scale, the decision authority (CTO), and the final decision with the reasoning: 'PostgreSQL chosen for ACID compliance requirements and team familiarity.' She has the full institutional reasoning in 2 minutes.

name: Consultant
definition: Intelligence consumer operating in Inquiry; Planning; Review; Simulation modes; every answer includes sources; confidence; reasoning; recommended action
purpose: Turn memory into decisions
outputs: Mode-specific outputs with sources and confidence
plain_english: Consultant is the Brain's conversational intelligence surface — where you go to ask questions, get structured plans, review progress against commitments, or explore scenarios. Unlike a general AI chat that answers from training data, the Consultant always answers from the Brain's actual organizational memory — every response is grounded in real Memory records, sourced, and traceable. It operates in four distinct modes: Inquiry (what do we know about this?), Planning (what should we do?), Review (are we on track?), and Simulation (what happens if we do X instead of Y?).
example: The VP of Sales asks Consultant: 'We have a board meeting in two weeks on Q3 performance. What should I prepare?' Consultant runs in Review mode: reads all Q3 goals, scans Commitment Memory for fulfillment rates across Q3 initiatives, pulls all open Operational Risks, checks active Drift Signals, and retrieves all current Recommendations directed at the Sales team. Response: 'Q3 commitment fulfillment: 71% (target: 85%). Critical risks to flag: Acme renewal at risk (high), 2 overdue enterprise commitments. Positive signals: win rate on RFPs submitted within 48hrs is up to 3.1x average. Recommended board narrative: [structured draft]. All figures sourced from Commitment and Action Memory, June 1–27.'

name: Agent System
definition: Assign to Agent available anywhere human can be assigned; categories: Support; Scheduling; Review; Execution; Research; Specialist
purpose: Turn memory into delegated execution
plain_english: Agent System is Mission Control's interface for overseeing, configuring, and managing AI agents that operate on the Brain's behalf. This is where humans set the explicit boundaries of agent autonomy — what agents are pre-authorized to do (Always tier), what requires human sign-off first (Ask First tier), and what is permanently blocked regardless of confidence (Never tier). It is also where humans review agent actions, respond to escalations, and audit what agents have done. The Agent System embodies the principle that AI autonomy is only trustworthy when it is explicitly bounded and continuously overseen.
example: A 'Renewal-Bot' agent is configured in Agent System for the Acme Corp account: Always tier — send standard meeting reminders, retrieve commitment status, read account history. Ask First tier — send any external email, update commitment status to Fulfilled, schedule meetings on behalf of account executives. Never tier — modify contract terms, approve exceptions, access payment data, contact CFO-level contacts without manager approval. When Renewal-Bot hits an edge case — the Acme contact replies asking to renegotiate contract scope — it stops, reports to Agent System: 'Action requires Ask First authorization: contract scope modification. Escalating to Account Executive Sarah.' Sarah approves or redirects.

name: Automation
