purpose: Turn recurring work into systems
lifecycle: Draft → Testing → Approval → Active → Paused → Archived
plain_english: Automation is Mission Control's interface for creating, managing, and monitoring rule-based workflows that run autonomously on the Brain's memory and intelligence. Where Agent System manages reasoning agents that exercise judgment, Automation manages deterministic rules: when X condition is true, do Y action. The Brain's Automations differ from traditional workflow tools because their triggers are organizational reality events — 'when a commitment breaches,' 'when a Brain Score drops below 60,' 'when a Drift Signal is confirmed' — rather than simple system events or calendar schedules.
example: An Automation is configured: 'Trigger: Any Commitment status changes to Breached AND related Goal impact is above $50k AND commitment owner has zero recorded activity in the last 72 hours. Action: (1) Notify commitment owner with full context. (2) Notify commitment owner's manager with Risk summary. (3) Auto-generate a follow-up Commitment assigned to manager: 'Review breached commitment and determine recovery plan within 48 hours.' (4) Flag in Operational Intelligence report. Owner: Operations Team.' This runs silently at scale across all commitments, catching organizational failures before they cascade — no human has to manually monitor each commitment.

outputs: Health dashboards; Velocity metrics; Drift monitor
plain_english: Operational Intelligence is Mission Control's strategic analytics and insight surface — where executives, operations leads, and department heads go to understand how the organization is functioning at a systemic level, above any individual person, team, or commitment. It aggregates Intelligence layer outputs across all scopes into views that answer strategic questions: Where are our processes breaking down repeatedly? Where are we underperforming against goals? What structural bottlenecks exist? What systemic opportunities are we missing? It is the difference between knowing what is wrong with one deal and knowing what is wrong with how we operate.
example: The VP of Operations opens Operational Intelligence for a monthly review. Sees: 'Process Bottlenecks: 5 active (3 in Legal review steps — averaging 11 days vs. 3-day SOP target; 2 in Finance approval — averaging 6 days vs. 2-day target). Drift Signals: 2 systemic (onboarding security review skip rate: 42%; proposal pricing approval bypass: 33%). Opportunity Signals: 1 high-confidence (enterprise deals with Legal involved from week 1 win at 2x rate — 14 confirmed instances). Brain Score trend: Organizational average declining from 74 to 67 over 30 days.' These are systemic insights — actionable at the structural level, not just the individual incident level.

name: Three-Tier Boundary System
definition: Always (pre-authorized); Ask First (approval required); Never (forbidden regardless of confidence); UI and config owned by Product; authority logic owned by Trust

conflict_flag: no — designed split; authority logic=TRU-COMP-007; UI=this row per T&G §8
plain_english: The Three-Tier Boundary System is the explicit governance framework that defines exactly what AI agents are authorized to do at any moment. Tier 1 — Always: actions pre-authorized for autonomous execution, no per-instance approval needed. Tier 2 — Ask First: actions that require explicit human approval before execution. Tier 3 — Never: actions permanently blocked regardless of agent confidence, context, or Readiness assessment. This framework is where human authority over agent behavior is made concrete and configurable — preventing both over-restriction (agents so constrained they are useless) and over-authorization (agents with more autonomy than is safe or appropriate).
example: Configuration for an onboarding agent: Always (pre-authorized) → read any new hire's role definition, retrieve standard equipment lists, send the template welcome email, schedule the day-1 orientation automatically. Ask First (requires Approval) → send customized onboarding emails with modified content, create commitments on behalf of the hiring manager, adjust the onboarding schedule, contact the new hire's future team members. Never (hard blocked) → modify compensation records, change system access permissions, send emails to executives, access financial or legal systems. These tiers are explicit, auditable, and configurable per agent scope — not inferred from confidence levels.
